sections.h: Asa in Chronicles: reform, victory, covenant
sections.b: Chronicles expands Kings' brief, positive account of Asa (1 Kings 15:9–24) into three chapters. Asa removes foreign altars and tells Judah to seek the LORD (14:2–5); he defeats Zerah the Cushite after a prayer of total dependence (14:9–15); and after Azariah son of Oded's sermon he leads a covenant in which Judah swears to seek the LORD with all its heart (15:1–15). He removes the queen mother Maacah, his grandmother on the usual reading, from her rank (15:16).

Kings tells of Asa's treaty with Ben-hadad of Damascus as a success (1 Kings 15:16–22). Chronicles adds Hanani the seer's rebuke: Asa leaned on Aram, not on the LORD (16:7–9). Asa imprisons the prophet, oppresses some of the people, and in his illness seeks healers, not the LORD (16:10–12). Chronicles still records his honorable burial (16:14). The word "lean" ties the story together (14:11; 16:7–8).

The dates in 15:19 and 16:1 conflict with Kings, where Baasha died in Asa's twenty-sixth year (1 Kings 16:8). Rabbinic chronology (Seder Olam) and some modern scholars count the years from the division of the kingdom; others assume a copying error (fifteenth and sixteenth); others see the Chronicler's own design of Asa's reign, with long faithfulness followed by a late fall. The Greek agrees with the Hebrew in 15:19 but has the thirty-eighth year in 16:1. See "Dating the Kings."

common: Asa was one of Judah's good kings whose faith weakened late in life.
uncommon: Some read Asa's foot disease (16:12) as a euphemism for a sexual disease, an old but minority view.

sections.b: Kings gives Jehoshaphat a short summary and a role in Ahab's and Joram's wars (1 Kings 22; 2 Kings 3). Chronicles gives him four chapters (17–20). He seeks God, removes high places, and sends officials, Levites and priests to teach the scroll of the law in Judah's towns (17:3–9). He appoints judges and charges them to judge for the LORD (19:4–11). Facing Moab and Ammon, he prays and wins a battle by sending singers ahead of the army (20:1–30).

Chronicles criticizes Jehoshaphat's ties with the north. His marriage alliance with Ahab (18:1) draws him into the battle at Ramoth-gilead, where he survives only because he cries out and God draws the enemy away (18:31). Jehu son of Hanani rebukes him for helping the wicked (19:2), and Eliezer condemns his shipping partnership with Ahaziah (20:35–37). The marriage of his son Jehoram to Athaliah brings Ahab's influence into Judah (21:6).

common: Jehoshaphat was a righteous king whose main fault was alliance with the wicked kings of Israel.
uncommon: Some scholars think the teaching mission and judicial reform were read back into his reign from his name, "the LORD judges."

sections.b: When Athaliah killed the royal family, Jehoshabeath hid the infant Joash in the Temple for six years (22:10–12). Jehoiada the priest gathered Levites and family heads, crowned and anointed him, and led a covenant that the people would be the LORD's (23:1–21). Chronicles retells 2 Kings 11 with Levites guarding the holy places and singers leading praise, so that no one but priests and Levites enters the house of the LORD (23:6).

Joash did right "all the days of Jehoiada the priest" (24:2). He organized the repair of the Temple with a chest at its gate (24:4–14). After Jehoiada's death he listened to the officials, Judah turned to Asherah poles and idols, and he ordered the stoning of Jehoiada's son Zechariah (24:17–22). Aram defeated Judah, and his servants killed him in his bed; he was not buried with the kings (24:23–25). Kings mentions the assassination but not its cause (2 Kings 12:20–21).

The Hebrew spells his name both ways, Joash and Jehoash, sometimes within one chapter (2 Kings 12:1; 2 Kings 12:19). Chronicles almost always uses Joash. The site follows the spelling of each verse, as it does for Jehoram and Joram, and notes the change where it occurs. Chronicles also names his mother, Zibiah of Beersheba (24:1), and lists his two wives, chosen for him by Jehoiada (24:3), a detail that shows the dynasty being rebuilt.

sections.h: The murder in the Temple court
sections.b: After Jehoiada's death, God's Spirit clothed his son Zechariah, who stood above the people and warned that because they had left the LORD, he had left them. At King Joash's command they stoned him in the court of the LORD's house. Dying, he said, "May the LORD see it, and may he seek it out" (24:22). Chronicles makes his blood the reason Joash was killed (24:25).

Jesus warned that the blood of all the prophets would be required of his generation, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah (Luke 11:50–51; Matthew 23:35). In the order the Talmud gives (Bava Batra 14b), Chronicles stands last, so many see the first and last murders of the Scriptures; the Aleppo and Leningrad codices, however, put Chronicles first among the Writings, and Uriah son of Shemaiah was killed later in time (Jeremiah 26:20–23). Matthew's "son of Berechiah" has been explained as a confusion with the prophet Zechariah (Zechariah 1:1), as Jesus' or Matthew's own identification, or as pointing to another Zechariah. See the chapter page on 2 Chronicles 24.
sections.refs: 2 Chronicles 24:20–22; Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51; Genesis 4:10; Zechariah 1:1; Jeremiah 26:20–23

sections.b: The Talmud and midrash tell that Zechariah's blood seethed in the Temple court until the Babylonians came, and that Nebuzaradan killed priests, young men and children over it until he himself repented, and count seven sins in his murder: a priest, a prophet, a judge, innocent blood, the Temple court profaned, on a Sabbath, on the Day of Atonement. The story was read on the fast of the ninth of Av as part of the explanation for the Temple's fall.

common: The Zechariah of Matthew 23:35 and Luke 11:51 is usually identified with Zechariah son of Jehoiada.
uncommon: Some identify him with Zechariah son of Bareis, killed in the Temple in AD 68 (Josephus, Jewish War 4.334–344).

sections.b: In Asa's reign Zerah the Cushite invaded Judah with an enormous army and was defeated at Mareshah (14:9–15). Some identify him with an Egyptian (perhaps Nubian) commander under Osorkon I; others with a Cushite tribe of the Negev near Gerar, which would explain the pursuit to Gerar and the herds and tents taken there (14:13–15; compare Habakkuk 3:7). Hanani later reminds Asa of this victory as proof that the LORD could be trusted (16:8). No outside record names Zerah, and his army of a million is one of Chronicles' large numbers.

"Seeking" (darash, biqqesh) the LORD is Chronicles' favorite measure of a king. Asa told Judah to seek the LORD and was given rest (14:4–7); Azariah son of Oded summed it up: "Seek him, and he will let you find him. Leave him, and he will leave you" (15:2); the people swore to seek him and "he let them find him" (15:12–15). Jehoshaphat sought his father's God (17:4) and set his heart to seek God (19:3), and Judah gathered to seek the LORD in danger (20:3–4). The failures are the same word reversed: Asa did not seek the LORD in his illness (16:12).

sections.b: In these chapters Chronicles adds whole episodes that Kings lacks: Abijah's sermon and victory (13), Zerah's invasion and Asa's covenant (14–15), Hanani's rebuke (16:7–10), Jehoshaphat's teachers, judges and singing army (17; 19–20), Elijah's letter (21:12–15), and Zechariah's murder (24:17–22). It copies others nearly word for word: Micaiah and Ahab (18 = 1 Kings 22), Athaliah's fall (22:10–23:21 = 2 Kings 11). The changes in the copied passages are telling: Levites replace foreign guards (23:6), Jehoshaphat is rescued by God (18:31), and kings' fates are tied to their faithfulness.

Chronicles names prophetic writings for these reigns: the commentary of the prophet Iddo (13:22), the records of Jehu son of Hanani "taken up into the scroll of the kings of Israel" (20:34), and "the commentary on the scroll of the kings" (24:27). Traditional readers take these as real sources beyond Kings; critical scholars debate whether they were independent works or names for Kings itself.

2 Chronicles 15:19 and 16:1 put Baasha's attack in Asa's thirty-sixth year, but by Kings Baasha died in Asa's twenty-sixth (1 Kings 16:8). Solutions: count from the division of the kingdom (Seder Olam, Thiele), making it Asa's sixteenth year; a scribal error; or the Chronicler's own arrangement of the reign into long peace and late failure. The Greek has the same numbers in 15:19 but the thirty-eighth year in 16:1.

2 Chronicles 22:2 says Ahaziah was forty-two when he began to reign, older than his father, who died at forty (21:20). Kings has twenty-two (2 Kings 8:26), and some Greek manuscripts have twenty. Most see a copying error; medieval Jewish commentators (Radak among them) counted the forty-two years from the start of Omri's dynasty, to which his mother belonged. The Plain English Translation keeps forty-two and explains it in a note.

Chronicles calls Athaliah "daughter of Omri" (22:2) and "that wicked woman" (24:7). Her marriage to Jehoram brings Ahab's ways to Judah (21:6), she counsels her son Ahaziah "to do evil" (22:3), and after his death she destroys the royal line (22:10). Chronicles follows 2 Kings 11 for her fall, but adds that her sons broke into the Temple and gave its holy things to the Baals (24:7).

Chronicles leaves out almost all of Ahab's story. He appears only where he touches Judah: his marriage alliance with Jehoshaphat, the war at Ramoth-gilead and his death (18:1–34, from 1 Kings 22). "Ahab's house" then becomes the name for the influence that corrupts Judah under Jehoram and Ahaziah (21:6, 13; 22:3–4, 7–8). Chronicles never tells of Naboth, Elijah's contest on Carmel or Jezebel's death; for its readers Ahab matters as the source of the corruption that nearly ended David's line.

Elijah's only appearance in Chronicles is a letter to Jehoram of Judah, condemning his idolatry and the murder of his brothers and announcing a disease of the bowels (21:12–15). Kings places Elijah's ascension before Jehoshaphat's death (2 Kings 3:11), so the letter raises a chronological question. Traditional answers: it was written before he was taken up, or delivered later; some think the reigns overlapped. Many critical scholars take it as the Chronicler's composition in Elijah's name.

Chronicles mentions Jehu son of Nimshi only as the one "the LORD had anointed to cut off Ahab's house," who kills Judah's officials and King Ahaziah (22:7–9). Chronicles presents Ahaziah's death as "God's doing" (22:7): he went to visit his uncle Joram and was caught in the judgment meant for Ahab's house. Kings has him wounded near Ibleam and dying at Megiddo (2 Kings 9:27); Chronicles has him found hiding in Samaria and brought to Jehu (22:9). It also cites a different Jehu, the prophet Jehu son of Hanani, who rebukes Jehoshaphat (19:2; 20:34).

Asa bought Ben-hadad of Damascus' help against Baasha (16:2–4), and Hanani told him that Aram's army had escaped him as a result (16:7). Ahab and Jehoshaphat fought Aram at Ramoth-gilead (18). Under Joash a small Aramean force defeated Judah's larger army as judgment (24:23–24), the reverse of Judah's victories against great odds (13:3; 14:9). Ahaziah of Judah joined Joram of Israel against Hazael at Ramoth-gilead (22:5).

Chronicles says Asa removed the high places (14:3, 5) and also that they were not removed (15:17), and says the same of Jehoshaphat (17:6; 20:33). Kings says only that they were not removed (1 Kings 15:14; 22:43). Explanations: foreign high places were removed but those for the LORD remained; the reform was not lasting; or "Israel" in 15:17 refers to the north.

sections.h: Prophets who confront kings in Chronicles
sections.b: 2 Chronicles 13–24 is full of prophets, most unknown from Kings: Azariah son of Oded (15:1–7), Hanani the seer (16:7–10), Micaiah (18), Jehu son of Hanani (19:2–3), Jahaziel the Levite (20:14–17), Eliezer son of Dodavahu (20:37), Elijah by letter (21:12–15), and Zechariah son of Jehoiada (24:20). They speak at turning points, and the king's response decides his fate. Von Rad called some of their speeches "Levitical sermons."
sections.refs: 2 Chronicles 15:1–7; 2 Chronicles 16:7–10; 2 Chronicles 18:1–27; 2 Chronicles 19:2–3; 2 Chronicles 20:14–17; 2 Chronicles 20:37; 2 Chronicles 21:12–15; 2 Chronicles 24:19–22

sections.b: Jehoshaphat appointed judges in the fortified towns and charged them that they judged for the LORD, not for people; with the LORD there is no crookedness, favoritism or bribery (19:5–7). In Jerusalem a court of Levites, priests and family heads heard appeals, with a priest over the LORD's matters and a ruler over the king's (19:8–11). The charge draws on Deuteronomy 1:17, 10:17 and 16:18–20.

Chronicles tells battles in which Judah wins by crying out to God: Abijah's against Jeroboam, with priests' trumpets and a war shout (13:14–16); Asa's against Zerah after prayer (14:11–12); and Jehoshaphat's against Moab and Ammon, where singers go ahead and the enemy destroys itself (20:21–23). Jahaziel's word, "The battle does not belong to you. It belongs to God" (20:15), echoes David before Goliath (1 Samuel 17:47) and Moses at the Sea (Exodus 14:13–14).

Levite singers appear at decisive moments: Jahaziel, a descendant of Asaph, prophesies victory (20:14); the Kohathite and Korahite Levites praise with a loud voice (20:19); singers go ahead of the army singing "Give thanks to the LORD, for his loyal love is forever" (20:21); and at Joash's coronation singers with instruments lead the praise (23:13). Jehoiada restores the order of praise "by David's direction" (23:18).

In these chapters the covenant with David is invoked in argument and in crisis. Abijah claims that the LORD gave the kingdom to David and his sons by "a covenant of salt" (13:5). Under Jehoram the LORD would not destroy David's house "because of the covenant he had made with David," having promised him a lamp for all time (21:7). When Athaliah destroyed the royal family, one child survived (22:10–12), and Jehoiada crowned him "as the LORD said of David's sons" (23:3).

sections.b: After Athaliah's sons damaged the Temple (24:7), Joash collected Moses' tax for the tent of the testimony with a chest at the Temple gate; workers restored God's house "to its right measure" and strengthened it, and the leftover silver made vessels for worship (24:4–14). The Temple court then became the scene of Zechariah's murder (24:21). Compared with Kings, Chronicles puts the Levites in charge of collection and the people giving gladly.

Abijah contrasts Judah's Aaronic priests with Jeroboam's self-appointed ones (13:9–11). Azariah recalls a time with "no priest who taught" (15:3), Jehoshaphat sends priests to teach (17:8) and judge (19:8). Jehoiada the priest preserves David's line, crowns Joash and restores the priestly and Levitical service (23:1–21), and is buried among the kings (24:16) because he had done good in Israel, toward God and his house.
sections.refs: 2 Chronicles 13:9–11; 2 Chronicles 15:3; 2 Chronicles 17:8–9; 2 Chronicles 19:8–11; 2 Chronicles 23:1–21; 2 Chronicles 24:15–16

sections.b: Chronicles treats the northern kingdom as rebels against David's house (13:5–7), yet still calls them "Israelites" and appeals to them (13:12). Northerners from Ephraim, Manasseh and Simeon defect to Asa "when they saw that the LORD his God was with him" (15:9). Jehoshaphat's alliances with the north are condemned (19:2; 20:37). Chronicles' Israel is always larger than Judah, and the way back stays open to anyone who returns to the LORD.

Micaiah sees the LORD's council, where a spirit offers to be a lying spirit in the mouth of Ahab's prophets (18:18–22, from 1 Kings 22:19–23). Interpreters have read it as a vision of God's sovereignty over judgment, as a parable, or (in the Talmud) as the spirit of Naboth. Chronicles copies it almost unchanged, so its theology here is Kings'. The scene shows God's judgment working through Ahab's own wish to hear good news.

sections.h: Zechariah, the last martyr in the Hebrew Bible's traditional order
sections.b: Zechariah son of Jehoiada is stoned in the Temple court for speaking God's word (24:20–22). Hanani had been imprisoned for the same reason (16:10), and Micaiah struck and jailed (18:23–26). Jesus names Zechariah as the end of the list of murdered righteous (Luke 11:51), and Hebrews remembers the faithful who were stoned (Hebrews 11:37). Chronicles makes the pattern explicit: the LORD sent prophets, the people would not listen (24:19), and the king who killed the messenger was himself killed for it (24:25).

Under Jehoram, Edom threw off Judah's rule and set up its own king (21:8–10, from 2 Kings 8:20–22). Edomites (Mount Seir) are also named among the invaders destroyed in Jehoshaphat's battle (20:10, 22–23). Jehoshaphat's prayer recalls that Israel spared Edom, Moab and Ammon on the way from Egypt (20:10; Deuteronomy 2:4–19), so their attack is ingratitude. Chronicles ties Edom's revolt and Libnah's to Jehoram's leaving the LORD (21:10).

The verb "lean" (sha'an) marks faith in Asa's reign: Judah won "because they had leaned on the LORD" (13:18); Asa prayed "we lean on you" (14:11); later he "leaned on the king of Aram" (16:7–8). Jehoshaphat put it in Isaiah's words: "Hold firm to the LORD your God, and you will be held firm" (20:20; compare Isaiah 7:9). The wordplay in Hebrew links believing and being held firm ('aman).

Chronicles gives Abijah 400,000 chosen men against Jeroboam's 800,000, with 500,000 Israelites killed (13:3, 17); Asa 580,000 against Zerah's "thousand thousands" (14:8–9); and Jehoshaphat five commanders with 1,160,000 men (17:14–18), close to David's census of 1,100,000 for Israel alone (1 Chronicles 21:5). These far exceed what Iron Age Judah could field. Readers take them as literal, as counts of elef units rather than thousands, as numbers damaged in copying, or as the Chronicler's deliberate way of showing that victory belongs to God, not to the larger army (13:8; 14:11).
